item.title: Andrej Karpathy says understanding of large language model capabilities is diverging sharply among different user groups [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Andrej Karpathy highlights a widening gap in shared understanding of large language model (LLM) capabilities, noting that about 75% of the global population has little to no interaction with LLMs, while a small fraction of professionals experience advanced, frontier-grade applications. He categorizes users into groups ranging from casual users who see LLMs as simple chatbots to a tiny elite using cutting-edge systems for complex tasks like software development and scientific research. Karpathy explains this divergence is driven by factors including the scale of problems tackled, domain-specific capability peaks in areas like math and coding, and varying levels of access to LLM technology. He emphasizes that while most people see only modest improvements, a small group is witnessing rapid, transformative impacts, creating a sharp funnel of understanding and experience with AI capabilities.

item.title: Sakana AI researchers introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS) for recursive self-improvement using collective intelligence in AI models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers at Sakana AI and UC Berkeley have developed Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), a method enabling AI models to recursively improve themselves by optimizing multi-agent workflows and distilling collective intelligence as a self-supervision signal. MASS uses a single language model to act as executor, optimizer, and evaluator, iteratively refining team workflows and learning from self-judged best executions to enhance performance on non-verifiable research tasks. The approach draws inspiration from human collective learning and scientific communities, where shared knowledge and division of labor drive progress. MASS's recursive loop involves the model optimizing its own workflows and evaluating results without external supervision, with progress measured by independent assessments from GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8. This method aims to advance AI beyond current human knowledge by enabling continual self-learning where the model is both the optimizer and evaluator.

item.title: Researchers introduce SpireBench to evaluate long-horizon strategic play of large language models using the game Slay the Spire [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SpireBench, a benchmark that tests the long-term strategic reasoning of large language models (LLMs) by having them play the full commercial deck-building game Slay the Spire at its highest difficulty. The study evaluated 20 LLMs, finding that while advanced models outperform heuristic baselines and match average human players, they still fall short of expert-level performance, especially as game length increases. Models tend to misjudge risk and rely on prior knowledge rather than learning from past runs, limiting their strategic adaptation. SpireBench provides a comprehensive framework to analyze where and why agentic models fail in extended strategic tasks, offering tools to dissect performance across different game stages and highlighting challenges in risk assessment and memory utilization. This benchmark is the first to give models access to the complete original game, enabling a detailed comparison with existing evaluation methods and advancing the study of long-horizon strategic reasoning in AI.

item.title: Researchers introduce VEPA, a verified evolving formal policy framework for deterministic lifelong guardrails in large language model agents interacting with sensitive resources [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed VEPA, a framework that enforces deterministic, inspectable guardrails for large language model (LLM) agents operating over sensitive data and mutable system states. VEPA uses executable symbolic rules as formal policies and adapts these policies during deployment by proposing verified updates guided by LLM feedback, ensuring conflict-free and evidence-supported rule activation to maintain safety and security. VEPA addresses limitations of existing adaptive guardrails that rely on LLM inference and can produce inconsistent decisions by combining formal verification with adaptive policy evolution. Evaluations on multiple benchmarks show VEPA outperforms baseline methods, maintaining effectiveness even under challenging conditions such as mixed data streams, corrupted feedback, and extended deployment horizons.

item.title: Researchers develop a multi-agent LLM system for automated tuning of specialized neural network components, improving performance across spiking neural networks and physics-informed neural networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework with distinct analyst, coder, and recorder roles to automate tuning of key components in specialized neural networks without altering overall architecture. The system operates in a semantically narrow code generation space and is validated on tasks including spiking neural network classification and solving differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). The approach outperforms baselines by significant margins, achieving up to 13 percentage points higher classification accuracy on MNIST and reducing error metrics by several orders of magnitude in physics-based tasks. This framework demonstrates transferable automated tuning across diverse neural network models while maintaining internal structure.

item.title: Adaptive DHiSparse supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV with load-adaptive residency, improving throughput and concurrency in long-context serving [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Adaptive DHiSparse is a new system designed to enhance long-context serving by supporting speculative decoding over a hierarchical sparse key-value (KV) memory structure that adapts residency based on load. It protects essential working sets, retains additional history when GPU memory is available, and recovers remaining data through exact fused retrieval, improving efficiency over previous methods like HiSparse, DSpark, and DFlash2. In tests with GLM-5.3 at 100K context and concurrency 128, Adaptive DHiSparse with DFlash2 achieved 793 output tokens per second per decode GPU, outperforming HiSparse by 1.45 times and non-speculative adaptive serving by 1.27 times. It also sustained up to four times the concurrency and increased output by 2.3 to 3.7 times under the same latency constraints. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, it delivered 1.85 times the output of resident serving with DSpark. Additionally, optional residency management reduced host fetches significantly at low load and freed memory under pressure.

item.title: Researchers propose critique-conditioned on-policy self-distillation to improve error localization and correction in reasoning models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate on-policy self-distillation, where a teacher model scores a student's rollout to provide token-level credit for reinforcement learning, and find that traditional scoring signals fail to localize errors or distinguish correct from incorrect reasoning traces. They identify this limitation as structural, since error localization requires a search process that scoring alone does not perform. To address this, they introduce critique-conditioned self-distillation, where the teacher first generates a critique of the rollout and then conditions its scoring on that critique, resulting in better error localization and corrective feedback that encourages backtracking tokens like "Wait" and "But." This approach improves model performance on math problems at test time and provides useful signals in cold-start reinforcement learning scenarios where verifiable rewards are sparse.

item.title: Kairos introduces a byte-level foundation model combining novel attention mechanisms and a multi-scale codec for multimodal data, with initial optimization tests on text [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Kairos presents a foundation model designed to process multiple data modalities at the byte level, integrating bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention, sliding-window attention, block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts feed-forward layer, and a multi-scale byte-level codec. The model is trained using a uniform-noise denoising objective over a shared byte space encompassing text, image, audio, video, lidar, and control streams. Initial experiments focus on convergence and optimization using text-only data, specifically overfitting a single 440-byte sentence with parameter counts ranging from 1 to 15 million.

item.title: AutoIndexer introduces flexible-order decoding by training causal models on chains of edits to enable post-generation token insertions, substitutions, and deletions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AutoIndexer is a generative model designed to overcome limitations of autoregressive decoding in handling non-causally ordered data by simulating a chain of edits that allows flexible modifications of prior outputs through token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model predicts marker tokens to open and close edits and moves a cursor within the token sequence, similar to a text editor, enabling it to revise outputs post hoc. Training involves perturbing ground-truth sequences with inverse chained edits, teaching the model to undo these perturbations, which enhances robustness to erroneous context and adaptability to tasks like code correction. The method demonstrates post-generation editing capabilities absent in most autoregressive and diffusion models without sacrificing performance on standard language model benchmarks, with code available on GitHub.

item.title: Researchers propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that uses backward revision to improve online adaptation in language model agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework designed to enhance continual learning in language model agents by incorporating backward revision alongside forward read and write under an online streaming protocol. This approach revises reflections based on feedback from each interaction, aiming to better capture information and adapt to distribution shifts without relying on replay or validation data. Across multiple benchmarks and language model backbones, ReHarness outperforms existing methods including raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based techniques, and prompt optimization. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces meaningful, source-grounded revisions, corrects outdated experiences, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.

item.title: Researchers propose REDaCT, an inference-time unlearning framework for large reasoning models that prevents reasoning collapse while removing forget-set information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce REDaCT (REgenerate via Detection and Corrective Tuning), a new method for unlearning in large reasoning models that avoids reasoning collapse by detecting and correcting sentences leaking forget-set information during inference. REDaCT uses a binary leak detector and an embedding optimization module to guide reasoning away from leaked information, maintaining coherent chain-of-thought and proper reasoning termination. Experimental results demonstrate that REDaCT outperforms existing unlearning methods by preserving reasoning quality while achieving perfect answer forgetting and near-perfect chain-of-thought forgetting. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further study and application.

item.title: Researchers introduce CoCoEvolve, a meta-reflective evolutionary optimizer that improves production AI systems across data agents, LLM data pipelines, and data engineering workflows [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present CoCoEvolve, an evolutionary optimizer using meta-reflection to improve production AI systems by selectively retrieving evidence from evolutionary history and probing live systems before proposing mutations. CoCoEvolve outperforms existing methods on benchmarks including DABStep, data-eng-bench, and HotpotQA, achieving higher accuracy and solve rates than prior baselines. The approach demonstrates the value of meta-reflection in optimizing complex AI workflows beyond traditional frontier-focused mutation methods.

item.title: COFFEQA introduces counterfactual-guided few-shot distillation to improve LLM question answering accuracy using validated factual-counterfactual pairs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: COFFEQA is a new method for knowledge distillation that trains smaller student models to mimic larger teacher models in question answering tasks using limited training samples. It leverages counterfactual examples-minimally modified contexts that change the teacher's answer-to provide additional supervision and improve distillation performance, addressing issues caused by uncertain samples near decision boundaries. The approach introduces a metric called Context Following Difficulty (CFD) to validate counterfactuals before distillation. Experiments on multiple in-domain and out-of-domain QA benchmarks with T5 and Qwen2.5 models show that COFFEQA outperforms traditional factual-only few-shot distillation methods under the same sample budget. For example, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves exact match and F1 scores by approximately 8.77 and 9.98 points respectively using 32 few-shot pairs with the T5 model. This work provides geometric insights into how factual-counterfactual pairs constrain the divergence between teacher and student decision boundaries, offering a more efficient and effective distillation strategy for generative question answering models in resource-constrained settings.

item.title: Researchers propose CIG-SFT, an information-theoretic supervised fine-tuning method that improves generalization in large language models without extra data or online rollouts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CIG-SFT, a supervised fine-tuning framework that estimates task-conditioned information gain for each demonstrated token to enhance post-training of large language models. This method compares token likelihoods from a frozen reference model with and without task input to quantify how much the task reduces uncertainty about decisions, then incorporates this into a KL-regularized projection for fine-tuning. CIG-SFT outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning and recent adaptive methods on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, showing stronger generalization to challenging evaluation distributions. The approach achieves these improvements without requiring additional training data or online rollouts, addressing limitations of forcing models to imitate fixed demonstrations that may interfere with pretrained behaviors.

item.title: Researchers introduce CoBe benchmark to evaluate models' zero-shot conversational counterfactual text editing across 2000 scenarios in healthcare, science, business, and daily life [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed the Counterfactual Benchmark (CoBe) to test language models' ability to perform counterfactual text editing, which involves revising text based on hypothetical changes while preserving unaffected facts. CoBe includes 2000 questions spanning multiple domains and assesses models' zero-shot performance in conversational settings, revealing that current models often default to associational text generation rather than maintaining causal consistency. The study found that performance does not reliably improve with larger model size or longer outputs, suggesting limitations stem from training objectives rather than model capacity.

item.title: Researchers introduce Agents' Last Exam benchmark to evaluate AI agents on long-term, economically valuable tasks across 13 industry clusters with over 1,000 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a new benchmark designed to assess AI agents on extended, economically significant real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Created with input from over 250 industry experts, ALE covers non-physical industries based on the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy and includes 55 subfields grouped into 13 industry clusters encompassing more than 1,000 tasks. Current results indicate that the most challenging tasks remain largely unsolved, with an average full pass rate below 1% across standard configurations. ALE is intended as a living benchmark that will expand continuously as new workflows and industries are added. Its goal is to bridge the gap between AI benchmark performance and meaningful economic impact, moving beyond traditional leaderboards to measure sustained performance on tasks relevant to GDP.

item.title: Researchers introduce an auditing framework that uses fine-tuning artifacts to reveal vulnerabilities in prompt injection defenses, raising attack success rates up to 96% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed an auditing framework that stress-tests prompt injection defenses in large language models before deployment by leveraging intermediate fine-tuning checkpoints as stepping stones for optimization-based attacks. This approach exposes genuine vulnerabilities that realistic adversaries could exploit, significantly increasing attack success rates against state-of-the-art defenses from near zero to as high as 96%. The study highlights that current evaluation methods may overestimate robustness and emphasizes the importance of rigorous pre-release testing to prevent real-world harm to users.

item.title: Researchers audit six large language models for intersectional disability bias in 2,820 hiring scenarios using new ABLEIST metrics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a comprehensive audit of six large language models (LLMs) across 2,820 hiring scenarios to evaluate bias against people with disabilities (PwD), focusing on intersectional factors such as gender and caste. They introduced ABLEIST, a set of metrics grounded in disability studies, to measure ableism and intersectional harms like tokenism and superhumanization in LLM outputs. The study found significant increases in ableism-related harms toward disabled candidates that many state-of-the-art models failed to detect. These harms were further amplified for disabled candidates marginalized by gender and caste, revealing critical blind spots in current AI safety tools and underscoring the need for intersectional evaluations of LLMs in high-stakes domains like hiring.

item.title: Researchers present COBALT, a contextual bandit learning method using offline trajectories to train large language models for multi-turn code generation, improving performance on LiveCodeBench [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce COBALT, a method that reuses offline multi-turn code generation trajectories to efficiently train large language models (LLMs) without costly online reinforcement learning. COBALT treats multi-turn code generation as a one-step recoverable Markov decision process, training LLMs to complete partial code trajectories through single-step generation. On the LiveCodeBench benchmark, COBALT improves performance of R1-Distill 8B and Qwen3 8B models by up to 9.0 and 6.2 absolute Pass@1 points, matching online reinforcement learning baselines. The study also shows COBALT enhances robustness against misleading execution feedback through perturbation analysis. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available.

item.title: Researchers propose PACT, a Privileged Trace Co-Training framework to improve multi-turn tool-use agents by combining reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning with expert trace optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce PACT, a training framework designed to enhance multi-turn tool-use agents that must reason, call tools, and adapt over multiple interaction turns. PACT uses expert traces only during training as optimization signals rather than during rollout, combining a trace-conditioned reinforcement learning surrogate and a component-aware supervised fine-tuning loss to guide learning while maintaining prompt-only rollout generation. Experiments on benchmarks including FTRL, BFCL, and ToolHop demonstrate that PACT outperforms strong supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning baselines. The approach reduces over-reliance on training-only trace context by incorporating prompt-only anchoring and standard reinforcement learning updates, highlighting the benefits of privileged trace co-training for multi-turn tool-use learning.

item.title: Study finds medical foundation models trained with label supervision converge less in image representation across modalities and datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated over 750,000 medical images from 14 datasets and 5 imaging modalities using 119 models to assess how similarly different medical foundation models represent images. They measured agreement by the overlap of nearest neighbors in model embeddings and found that models trained with label supervision showed the least convergence, especially in chest radiography and histopathology, compared to models trained with self-distillation, masked image modeling, or contrastive pretraining. Agreement depended more on dataset source and imaging view than on diagnostic findings and was not strongly linked to accuracy. The study also demonstrated that a linear mapping between embeddings of two models could transfer classifiers for multiple chest findings with high accuracy, suggesting practical interoperability despite differences in model representations. The findings imply that developers can influence model convergence through pretraining objectives, and users might test successor models on unlabeled images to verify consistency before replacement.

item.title: OpenCollab launches a multi-agent coding framework with programmable collaboration and controllable runtime, achieving up to 97.2% adherence and new state-of-the-art performance in benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenCollab introduces a unified multi-agent coding framework designed to improve collaboration in complex software engineering tasks by providing programmable collaboration and a controllable runtime environment. The framework enforces experimental control, tracks execution through detailed event streams, and quantifies adherence to declared organizational structures, revealing significant variation in agent collaboration across configurations. Experiments show that OpenCollab's Duo configuration outperforms existing multi-agent coding systems such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, while its single-agent setup uses fewer tokens across evaluated benchmarks. This framework establishes a controlled infrastructure for programmable collaboration and causal evaluation in multi-agent coding systems.

item.title: Position paper outlines five key shortcomings of current Explainable AI faithfulness metrics for feature importance and proposes four research directions to improve their reliability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent position paper examines the limitations of faithfulness metrics used to evaluate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods that provide feature importance explanations. The authors argue that while XAI aims to build trust by making machine learning models more interpretable, current approaches often oversimplify model behavior, leading to unfaithful explanations that do not accurately reflect the model's decision process. The paper identifies five major structural misalignments in existing faithfulness metrics, which make rigorous quantification of explanation trustworthiness computationally expensive or infeasible. The authors propose four avenues for future research to address these shortcomings and enhance the reliability of faithfulness measurements. They emphasize that improving these metrics is crucial for advancing the trustworthiness and practical utility of XAI tools, which currently function more effectively as debugging aids than as definitive explanations for model predictions.

item.title: Study finds Monte Carlo Tree Search underperforms randomized-restart list scheduling by 2.88% on DAG workflow scheduling with equal computational budgets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A controlled study compared Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and randomized-restart list scheduling methods for scheduling directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflows using identical computational budgets. At a budget of 2048 evaluated schedules, MCTS performed about 2.88% worse than randomized restarts, with the performance gap not attributable to insufficient budget. The study tested workflows with up to 32 tasks and 8 processors in synthetic domains, finding that restarts outperformed MCTS on sparse irregular workflows, while no significant difference appeared on regular layered workflows and dense workflows showed limited room for improvement. Using a textbook UCT selection rule reduced MCTS's deficit but did not reverse it. The results do not extend claims to larger-scale or higher-budget scenarios.

item.title: Researchers develop MagicBeanStalk, a recursive data synthesis algorithm to improve reinforcement learning with verifiable reasoning by generating balanced, challenging training problems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced MagicBeanStalk, an algorithm that generates training problems calibrated to a target policy and training budget to enhance reinforcement learning with verifiable reasoning (RLVR). They identified that existing large math problem datasets often fall into a 'zero-advantage trap,' where most problems are either always solved or always failed, limiting learning effectiveness. MagicBeanStalk overcomes this by recursively expanding seed problems into diverse families that preserve reasoning structures while maintaining balanced difficulty. Experiments on eight math benchmarks showed that training on MagicBeanStalk problems significantly improved model performance compared to existing datasets, with gains of 8.6 points for gpt-oss-120b and 5.4 points for DeepSeek v4Flash on a 16K-token budget. The approach was also applied in finance, synthesizing over 14,000 verifiable problems from 340 solutions and achieving notable improvements on financial reasoning benchmarks SecQue and FinanceBench.

item.title: Researchers introduce SmartSalesBench, a multi-turn benchmark evaluating LLM sales agents against resistant buyer personas across 13,680 sessions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: SmartSalesBench is a new benchmark designed to test large language model (LLM) sales agents in conversations with psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas over up to twenty turns. Unlike existing benchmarks that assume cooperative users, this benchmark challenges agents with resistance and includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products, and multiple price tiers. The study involved four controlled experiments with three iterations totaling 13,680 sessions, using retrieval-augmented generation for both agent and persona creation. Evaluation metrics cover primary outcomes, quality measures, and exploratory metrics, combining automated LLM-as-judge scoring with human assessments showing strong agreement and correlation.

item.title: Researchers benchmark hyperbolic and Euclidean VAEs for unsupervised patent claim classification, finding hyperbolic models retrieve 52% more cross-category prior art on 45,000 US patents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers trained hyperbolic and Euclidean Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) on 45,000 US patents to evaluate unsupervised patent claim classification and prior-art retrieval. The hyperbolic model retrieved genuinely cross-category prior art 52% more often than the Euclidean model, despite aligning less with official classification codes, highlighting different goals between classification and search needs. The study also analyzed 10 technology domains with 50,000 additional patents, finding that a domain's classification breadth and patents per subgroup predict model performance. The researchers provide a 91-test automated implementation and report all findings with statistical transparency to guide practitioners on where the method is most valuable.

item.title: Researchers introduce a scalable method to maximize agent empowerment by increasing executable skills from a state, enabling emergent behaviors in complex environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present a scalable approach to empowerment maximization, defining empowerment as the number of executable skills available from a given state. This method applies to various skill learning techniques and allows studying empowerment beyond simple tabular settings. Experiments demonstrate that maximizing empowerment leads to emergent behaviors such as resource gathering, environment modification, and survival strategies, including building structures in the Crafter environment.

item.title: Researchers introduce EmbodiedCLBench, a benchmark for evaluating continual learning in self-evolving embodied agents using compositional generalization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark designed to assess continual learning capabilities in self-evolving embodied agents within simulated environments. The benchmark focuses on whether agents can learn basic tasks and recombine those skills to solve more complex, unseen tasks, highlighting the challenge of transferring experience in embodied settings. Extensive experiments using EmbodiedCLBench revealed that while agents struggle with zero-shot performance on advanced tasks, prior experience with basic tasks consistently improves outcomes. However, this improvement does not scale with additional learning samples, indicating current agents have limited ability to extract meaningful information from increased experience. The benchmark aims to support the development of more effective continual learning methods for embodied agents, with code and datasets publicly available.

item.title: Researchers introduce ReTRAIL framework enabling long-horizon language model agents to rewind environment states while preserving learned knowledge to improve exploration and task solving [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present ReTRAIL, a framework designed for large language model agents operating in long-horizon environments where early errors can cause cascading failures. ReTRAIL allows agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while retaining knowledge from abandoned explorations, enabling better recovery and guidance for future decisions. The framework trains a shared policy using State-Anchored GRPO and a branch-advancement reward to improve execution and exploration progress. Experiments on benchmarks including MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind function offers limited or negative effects, whereas ReTRAIL's combination of rewinding and experience reuse helps agents avoid unproductive states and leverage insights from previous attempts. This approach demonstrates the benefit of integrating environment rewinding with knowledge retention for solving complex, long-horizon tasks.

item.title: Researchers conduct black-box causal audit revealing model-dependent audio grounding in hallucinations of large audio-language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a black-box causal test to analyze object hallucination in large audio-language models (LALMs), isolating evidence regions via CLAP similarity and spectral gating across multiple models. They find that localization of evidence improves detection when controlling for duration, but detection effectiveness varies by model, with no unified causal-grounding profile transferable between models. The study also shows that combining contrastive decoding methods improves accuracy on Qwen2-Audio-7B from 57.1% to 71.9%, outperforming previous mitigation techniques. Source code and detailed findings are publicly available.

item.title: KnowForge introduces role-specialized agents for open-domain multimodal document QA, improving F1 scores by up to 11 points on M3DocVQA and outperforming prior RAG models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: KnowForge is a new pipeline for question answering over large, heterogeneous document collections that separates tasks among specialized agents: a Locator for searching, a Judge for bridging retrieval hops, a Deep Reader for reading text, images, and tables, and a synthesizer for answer formatting. Using a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model, KnowForge achieves an F1 score of 47.5 on the M3DocVQA benchmark, surpassing previous systems by significant margins and reaching 73.5 accuracy on MultiHop-RAG. The system's design includes a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index and a typed evidence pool that merges search rankings. Ablation studies show the Deep Reader's contribution varies with the visual content of datasets, and combining agents into one reduces performance due to excessive searching. KnowForge's query latency depends on model calls rather than corpus size. The authors provide free access to the indexed benchmarks, along with all prompts and runner code for reproducibility.

item.title: Researchers propose Foresight, an anticipatory generative model for road-network trajectories that improves next transition selection by incorporating future route anticipation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Trajectory generation is crucial for urban applications like traffic management and planning, but existing models often fail to accurately predict vehicle transitions at intersections, sometimes producing unrealistic paths off the road network. This paper introduces Anticipatory Generative Modeling, a new graph-constrained approach that models behavior on road networks by anticipating how future routes may unfold toward destinations. The proposed model, Foresight, uses a probabilistic "anticipate--select--update--re-anticipate" loop to enable longer-term foresight while generating sequential trajectories. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Foresight outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in trajectory generation tasks, addressing limitations of prior diffusion-based methods that simulate location sequences without effective next transition selection. This approach represents a shift from location simulation to behavior modeling, improving the realism and accuracy of generated vehicle trajectories within road networks.

item.title: JANUS framework enhances long-horizon autonomous research by co-evolving world models to forecast outcomes and refine candidate selection, improving efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: JANUS is a new framework designed to accelerate long-horizon autonomous research by integrating future outcome forecasting with past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. It enables a research agent to propose candidates that the world model evaluates for value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility before execution, reducing costly trial-and-error feedback delays. The system distills experience into evolving hierarchical skills for the research agent and exploration strategies for the world model, allowing continual co-evolution that sharpens candidate generation and predictive judgment over extended horizons. Evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks show JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both evolving efficiency and performance ceiling.

item.title: BoundaryEvo introduces a two-stage data-model co-evolution framework to improve long-chain reasoning in small language models, adapting training data to evolving model capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: BoundaryEvo proposes a novel approach to distilling long-chain reasoning from large teacher models to smaller language models by adapting training data as the student model's reasoning capability evolves. The framework includes Capability Priming, where a small set of teacher-generated reasoning trajectories are distilled without filtering, and Capability-Boundary Co-Evolution, which iteratively selects training examples that challenge but are solvable by the student model. Using only 1,000 training examples, BoundaryEvo significantly improves accuracy on 11 reasoning benchmarks, including raising Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 62.9 to 75.3 on IMO-AnswerBench and from 26.8 to 46.0 on AMO-Bench. The authors plan to release the code and data publicly.

item.title: ChemDiffAgent introduces masked diffusion language model for tool-integrated chemical reasoning, outperforming autoregressive agents by 20% across six chemistry tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present ChemDiffAgent, a masked diffusion language agent designed to improve chemical reasoning by integrating external tools through iterative denoising and full-trajectory context. This approach addresses limitations of autoregressive models in bidirectional molecular understanding, coordinated tool planning, and multi-source evidence integration. The team developed a two-stage post-training framework to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities and evaluated the model on a benchmark covering six chemistry tasks involving single-turn and multi-turn tool use. ChemDiffAgent's 8 billion parameter model achieves performance comparable to or exceeding larger models like GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7, demonstrating significant improvements in chemical reasoning tasks.

item.title: SqueezeBench launches a saturation-resilient benchmark for AI mathematical capability using machine-checked proofs and incremental record improvements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: SqueezeBench introduces a new benchmark designed to measure AI progress in mathematics without saturation by raising the difficulty bar with each success. It uses integer functions with known values for small inputs and maintains lower and upper bounds verified by machine-checked proofs in the Lean theorem prover. Submissions propose improved bounds that must be strictly better at some point, with proofs checked independently to ensure correctness and prevent trivial exhaustive searches. The benchmark includes ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty initial records and tools for submission and verification. Baseline agents using a frontier language model improved every record with 82 accepted submissions, while newer models further improved 19 of 20 records with 60 additional accepted submissions. For most problems, some records remain asymptotically behind the best published bounds, indicating room for further AI-driven mathematical advances.

item.title: Researchers introduce PRISM, a retrieval-augmented multimodal language model integrating heterogeneous clinical data for prognosis, achieving high AUROC scores on MDS-ED and external MC-MED benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model designed to integrate structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context for clinical prognosis. PRISM uses per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank that retrieves mean-pooled embeddings of similar patient encounters without including individual records in prompts. On the 1,443-task MDS-ED benchmark, PRISM achieved AUROCs of 86.2% for diagnosis, 93.1% for deterioration, 91.8% for ICU admission, and 92.8% for mortality using a 96-hour pre-arrival window unavailable to prior baselines. Comparisons show PRISM outperforms a compact fusion model using the same evidence streams and frozen encoders, and replacing numerical EHR encoding with text serialization or removing pre-arrival history reduces performance. Genuine retrieval also outperforms random-neighbor retrieval, though statistical significance is marginal. On the external MC-MED cohort, supervised fine-tuning of PRISM reached 0.8611 AUROC, surpassing locally trained gradient boosting and source-only PRISM models. These results support the effectiveness of structure-aware multimodal integration and supervised external adaptation for clinical prognosis.

item.title: Researchers introduce UkrMeme dataset and evaluate vision-language models for detecting persuasive techniques in Ukrainian wartime memes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a propaganda benchmark preserving original visuals. They evaluate vision-language models in zero-shot setups across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. The study also compares explanation methods, including Layer-wise Relevance Propagation and model-generated token attributions, analyzing the semantic evidence each emphasizes.

item.title: Researchers propose PAGE framework using AI to analyze 3,929 American comics and 87 Japanese manga volumes, enabling large-scale study of visual and textual elements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce PAGE, an AI-based framework that parses comic scans into panels, text, and bibliographic data, annotates pages with vision-language models, and grounds findings in human annotation to study comics at scale. They demonstrate PAGE on nearly 4,000 American comic books from 1938 to 1956 and 87 volumes of Japanese manga through three studies examining political power portrayal, visual style across artists, and speech patterns across traditions. The framework aims to transform comics scholarship from isolated book studies to comprehensive archive analysis, offering tools to make comics searchable by content, accessible to blind and low-vision readers, and aiding preservation and artist crediting. The researchers outline a future research agenda where AI enhances the study, preservation, and accessibility of comics as a cultural medium.

item.title: Researchers propose IG-VLA framework for efficient vision-language-action reasoning by internalizing future scene imagination, achieving up to 6% success improvement and 6.38x speedup on robotic tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce IG-VLA, a vision-language-action reasoning framework that enables models to internally imagine future scene evolution in latent space, guiding robotic action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. The approach includes Scene Gist Memory, which compresses reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact token to reduce inference overhead. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench benchmarks show that IG-VLA's reasoning and gist policies outperform strong baselines by nearly 6% in success rate, with the gist policy achieving up to 6.38 times faster inference, reducing latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that internalized future spatiotemporal reasoning can improve both effectiveness and efficiency in robotic manipulation tasks.

item.title: Researchers develop CircuitTree to compose multiple neural circuits into a syllable transcriber achieving 64.8% accuracy with shared components [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose CircuitTree, a new method and data structure for composing many modular neural circuits into a single model, overcoming limitations of naive circuit union. They applied this to circuits pruned from HuBERT phoneme classifiers, combining 39 phoneme circuits into a syllable classifier that transcribes open syllables with 64.8% accuracy, close to a 66.0% ceiling without shared circuitry. The approach shares 99.5% of circuit components, demonstrating efficient hierarchical composition of interpretable subnetworks for speech tasks.

item.title: Researchers study self-preservation in language models using generated replay and task selection to reduce forgetting during continual learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate how language models can preserve their capabilities during continual learning by generating replay data and selecting preservation tasks without access to original training data. They organize task descriptions into Task Banks to guide replay generation and test this approach on Qwen models of various sizes. The study finds that replay reduces forgetting beyond the tasks in the bank, combining partial banks improves retention, and models can help choose replay targets to enhance preservation, especially in larger models. The findings suggest that language models can support broader self-preservation by generating and selecting replay tasks, balancing preservation with learning new tasks under fixed example budgets.

item.title: Researchers benchmark machine learning and time-series foundation models for day-ahead electricity forecasting in a university building, finding TimesFM 3.0 with covariates reduces mean absolute error by 43% compared to seasonal-naive methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated statistical, machine-learning, recurrent neural network, and pretrained TimesFM models for forecasting day-ahead electricity demand in a university building. They used chronological validation over 57 test days, comparing accuracy across workdays, weekends, and holidays, while considering local fitting and forecasting time. TimesFM 3.0 with weather covariates achieved the lowest overall errors, though XGBoost remained competitive without a clear advantage in mean absolute error. TimesFM performed well using only past electricity consumption, with covariates improving holiday forecasts but slightly worsening others. TimesFM requires no building-specific training, whereas XGBoost offers rapid local fitting and inference; an LSTM model took longer to train without outperforming these approaches. Additional analyses revealed seasonal variation in electricity demand and showed that different weather data sources had minimal impact on TimesFM accuracy. The findings suggest pretrained TimesFM as a strong baseline for building electricity forecasting, with XGBoost as a viable locally fitted alternative. Incorporating covariates is particularly beneficial when improved holiday forecasts justify the extra input preparation.

item.title: Researchers present Cancerous Backdoor Attack that gradually corrupts large language models' reasoning using invisible tokens and a stage controller [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce the Cancerous Backdoor Attack, a method that gradually corrupts reasoning in large language models (LLMs) through multiple stages using invisible tokens and a stage controller that tracks attack progression during inference. This approach contrasts with typical backdoor attacks that activate a single terminal behavior upon trigger satisfaction. The attack was evaluated across several reasoning datasets and consistently produced gradual reasoning corruption across different models and tasks. Compared to prior backdoor attack methods, Cancerous Backdoor Attack outperforms baselines and reveals that reasoning corruption can develop before becoming visible, indicating that answer accuracy alone may be insufficient for detecting such attacks.

item.title: Researchers propose Kronecker Product Attention for memory-efficient key-value cache compression in autoregressive models, achieving up to 10x reduction with maintained or improved accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), a method that compresses key and value activations in autoregressive generation models by representing them as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA generalizes previous approaches like Tensor Product Attention and incorporates a structured rotary embedding operator to preserve relative positional information without extra components. Empirical results show that KPA matches or outperforms existing attention mechanisms across multiple model scales and benchmarks while significantly reducing memory usage by up to tenfold. The approach includes a tunable hyperparameter allowing users to balance compression and accuracy without altering model architecture.

item.title: GeoFitBench-LLM benchmark assesses large language models' ability to infer geospatial data requirements for geo-analytic tasks, with GPT-5.4 Thinking recovering full resource sets in 66.67% of cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their capability to identify necessary datasets, supporting resources, and constraints from natural language geo-analytic requests. The benchmark focuses on two reasoning dimensions-Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding-addressing key challenges in geospatial information retrieval. Experiments with seven LLMs under minimal prompting show that while resource identification is often achievable, accurately specifying fitness-for-use remains challenging as inferential complexity increases. GPT-5.4 Thinking performed best, fully recovering required resources in two-thirds of the benchmark requests.

item.title: Researchers develop unsupervised multimodal reward model using a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone and perturbation-based training, outperforming GPT-4o on several benchmarks with minimal fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have created a vision-language reward model that requires no human preference labels by training a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone to score original web captions higher than perturbed versions. This approach, which uses perturbations instead of annotated preference pairs, achieves better or comparable performance to GPT-4o on three benchmarks, including a 6.6-point lead on VL-RewardBench, while using significantly less fine-tuning compute. The model's success hinges on selecting the optimal intermediate layer, which improves performance by 5.8 points over the last layer. Training with perturbations yields 3 to 5 points more improvement than curated preference pairs, and retraining the head on verifier-labeled candidates reduces caption hallucination and improves image-generation pass rates. This method offers a cost-effective, annotator-free recipe for multimodal reward modeling that is defined by the training comparisons rather than benchmark rankings.

item.title: Researchers introduce KITE, a knowledge-injected temporal encoder for forecasting rare events in multivariate time-series using semantic priors and switchable mechanisms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present KITE, a self-supervised event forecaster that incorporates semantic priors-expert knowledge absent from scarce labels-into time-series forecasting through two switchable mechanisms: a covariate mechanism and an attention-bias mechanism. This approach improves prediction of rare, high-cost events by supplementing limited data with contextual knowledge without requiring per-dataset architecture changes. Experiments show that informative priors enhance in-domain forecasting accuracy and transfer effectively across domains, while priors redundant with observed data have no effect. KITE offers a flexible framework for contextual conditioning and aims to support scalable, cross-domain pretrained time-series models with explicit governing structures.

item.title: Researchers develop WZDrive, a multimodal ego-trajectory predictor for autonomous driving in urban work zones using human-in-the-loop simulator data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address the challenge of predicting vehicle trajectories in urban roadway work zones by collecting WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset from 33 drivers using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with VR-controlled workers. Their proposed model, WZDrive, improves prediction accuracy by reducing key error metrics compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The study fills a gap in autonomous driving research by combining human driving signals and multimodal learning to better handle the complexities of temporary lane changes and interactions in work zones.

item.title: When Generative Models Act as Simulators [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.12847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A simulator summarizes an environment in a state that users can read and change. Generative models learn representations of the world without explicit specification, but offer no built-in way to edit that world's state. We investigate the conditions under which a generative model can act as a simulator through $\textit{editability}$: whether changing a model's latent representation produces the next-step outputs we get by editing a simulator's state. Plainly stated, our goal is to find a mapping between a generative model's latent state and the simulator state, where the model is trained on observations alone and the mapping is learned afterward. We test two kinds of mappings, both learned from observations paired with simulator states. In one, we train probes to decode the simulator state from the model, then steer along them. In the other, we learn the mapping directly with an inverse map, which can succeed even where steering fails. We study both in two contrasting environments: the discrete board game Othello, and Rayworld, our own continuous world of moving discs seen through partial renderings, closer to physical scenes and video. We find that which mapping succeeds depends strongly on the environment, even though the state is decodable in every variant. In Othello, editability falls smoothly as the game is simplified, and even small rule changes have large consequences. In Rayworld, probes fail to steer along the simulator's continuous state, yet an inverse map sets the model from that state anyway. A model can therefore be driven by a simulator it may have never learned.

item.title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.12939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.

item.title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.12957v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.

item.title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.

item.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13035v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.

item.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

item.title: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP

item.title: ReSFlow: Rectifying Categorical Flows on Statistical Manifolds for One-Step Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative modeling for discrete data has been significantly advanced by learning continuous vector fields on the statistical manifolds to transport simple priors to target discrete distributions. However, because these continuous-time flows are not constrained to follow geodesics on the statistical manifold, thereby requiring multi-step numerical integration for simulation and leading to substantial computational costs during inference. In this work, drawing inspiration from the "straight and fast" properties of Rectified Flow in continuous Euclidean space, we propose the Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow) model, which enables one-step categorical generation on statistical manifolds by explicitly learning geodesic trajectories that adhere to the intrinsic Riemannian geometry. By rectifying the flow on the statistical manifold, we theoretically guarantee that trajectories between prior and target distributions approximate geodesics. This rectification significantly reduces the transport cost by aligning the learned trajectories directly along geodesics on the statistical manifold, allowing the model to map pure noise to target discrete data in a single step. Through extensive experiments on diverse real-world generative tasks, ranging from image and text to biological domains, we demonstrate ReSFlow's superior one-step generation quality, which truly embodies geodesically optimal and rapid categorical generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaohuanjia/ReSFlow.

item.title: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved the performance of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers, yet determining when their outputs can be trusted remains largely unexplored. This work presents the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting using top-k beam-search candidates. Uncertainty is estimated from pairwise candidate similarities and evaluated using the Prediction Rejection Ratio. This work characterises the relationship between parsing performance and uncertainty, evaluates the reliability of beam candidate distributions, analyses the effect of evaluation metrics on uncertainty assessment, and identifies parsers that provide the strongest balance between performance and reliability. Experimental results show the value of uncertainty estimation as a complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers.

item.title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.

item.title: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM judges are increasingly deployed as panels, and disagreement among panel members is often read as a symptom of an unclear rubric. We test a label-free procedure that turns this disagreement into rubric repairs. The procedure decomposes each rubric into sub-criteria, ranks them by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and has an editor model rewrite only the most contested ones. An additional stage that moves text-checkable sub-criteria to deterministic checkers transferred none in our evaluation. Human labels are never used to select or edit clauses; they are used only to evaluate the outcome. We pre-specified four hypotheses in a version-controlled protocol and evaluated six rubric conditions with a panel of five judges from three providers on SummEval, the HealthBench meta-evaluation, and USR Topical-Chat, for a total of 129,770 judge requests, excluding retries. On SummEval, the procedure raised inter-judge Krippendorff's $\alpha$ by 0.069 (95% CI 0.046 to 0.092) over the original rubric and by 0.074 over a control that applied the same edits to an equal number of randomly chosen clauses that were not selected. Agreement with expert ratings showed no detectable change (Kendall $\tau$ difference -0.007, 95% CI -0.037 to 0.021). On HealthBench and USR, neither inter-judge agreement nor human agreement met the preregistered effect criteria. In a preregistered secondary comparison, human agreement after editing the contested clauses was lower than after editing the control clauses on all three datasets in point estimate, although no interval excluded zero. Selecting clauses by disagreement makes judges agree with each other more than editing arbitrary clauses does, but in our setting the added consensus did not bring the judges closer to human annotators. We will release code, frozen rubrics, item identifiers, and judge scores.

item.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.

item.title: ProgramGym: Scaling Training Environments for Long-Horizon Program Reproduction Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to build programs from scratch as software engineers do rather than to resolve issues within a repository or to generate a repository from a given requirements document. However, scalable verifiable training environments that force agents to discover what is required and to decide how the system should be designed remain scarce. Moreover, existing agent workflows also cannot sustain long-horizon development in which the agent explores the reference program before implementation. To address these challenges, we introduce ProgramGym, a framework consisting of Program-Env and Program-Agent for scalable training environments of long-horizon program reproduction agents. Specifically, Program-Env constructs verifiable training environments from repositories through a feedback-driven loop that repairs runtime sandbox builds and the quality of black-box tests. Using this novel pipeline, we obtain 1,648 training environments spanning C, C++, Go, and Rust. Program-Agent combines a role-isolated workflow of analysis, implementation, and review with revision management for compilation checks and failure recovery. Experiments on ProgramBench show that both Program-Env and Program-Agent improve performance on program reproduction. Fine-tuning on trajectories with these constructed environments raises the performance of Qwen3.8-27B from 34.87% to 42.84%. Program-Agent further raises the base and SFT models to 55.71% and 56.25%, both exceeding some flagship models. We will release the ProgramGym to support further research on coding agents that build programs from scratch.

item.title: In-Context Learning for System Identification: Probabilistic Formulation, Long-Sequence Handling, and Benchmark Validation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional system identification typically involves two steps: initially, training data is processed to estimate a model of the system of interest; then, the model is used to predict outputs for new input queries. In contrast, recent in-context learning approaches learn a meta model that maps directly from training data and query inputs to outputs in a zero-shot fashion, bypassing explicit model estimation. This approach leverages a meta model trained offline, on large sets of synthetically generated data, to emulate the behavior of a system identification algorithm. In this work, we advance this meta-learning framework for system identification in three directions. First, we develop a unified probabilistic meta-identification architecture that combines a Transformer-based encoder-decoder with tailored mechanisms for handling long training sequences, enabling calibrated predictions over long horizons. Second, we show how a pre-trained meta model can act as an uncertainty-aware synthetic data generator for classical system identification, providing task-specific data that regularize parametric models when real data are scarce. Third, we systematically evaluate the framework on standard nonlinear system identification benchmarks and on a challenging out-of-distribution scenario, demonstrating competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art methods and strong generalization, including cases where input-only adaptation is sufficient to handle significant distribution shifts.

item.title: Beyond Temporal Proximity: Explanatory World Models for Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative Recommenders increasingly use Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize outcomes that may appear hundreds or thousands of interactions after a decision. Standard RL propagates reward according to temporal proximity rather than explicit relevance, attenuating the signal assigned to distant but important actions and creating a source of sample inefficiency. We introduce Explanatory World Models (EWM), an attribution framework that uses explanations to identify the earlier events that plausibly contributed to a realized outcome. We instantiate EWM with a frontier language model and use its explanations as learning signals using a conservative hierarchical operator that recursively redistributes reward while preserving the undiscounted episode return. To investigate what constitutes a useful explanation, we operationalize three complementary variants inspired by Halpern's actual causation, Lombrozo's explanatory simplicity, and Deutsch's hard-to-vary explanations. We evaluate EWM on two controlled long-horizon RL benchmarks, a public sequential-recommendation benchmark, and an industry-scale generative recommender. On Crafter and WordCraft, EWM substantially outperforms PPO and LaRe, with its largest gains when rewards are most delayed. On KuaiRand, EWM outperforms SFT and LaRe offline and A2C online. Finally, in an offline evaluation of an industry generative recommender, EWM considerably improves Recall and increases behavioral proxies. These results suggest that explanations can provide structured and reusable credit for learning from delayed outcomes.

item.title: Defence against the dark arts of distillation: Unsupervised discovery of subliminal learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13536v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a language model is distilled from a teacher that shares its base parameters, the student can inherit behavioural traits of the teacher---including misalignment---even from data that is semantically unrelated to the trait (Cloud et al., 2026). All existing defences require knowing the trait. We remove this requirement and prove that a subliminally transferred trait can be recovered from the parameter updates alone, without supervision, by exploiting a single asymmetry: the trait is expressed consistently across diverse datasets generated by the teacher, whereas task-specific and shared capabilities vary. The resulting estimator returns a weight-space direction that can be amplified to discover and interpret the trait or projected out to suppress it. Applied to the subliminal-learning benchmarks of (Cloud et al., 2026), our method recovers the transmitted animal-preference traits without any trait labels and suppresses their expression with almost no impact to task performance.

item.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2610.13644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications.
